<strong>Présentée jusqu’au 20 décembre à: On view until December 20 at McGill’s Islamic Studies Library, the installation The Arab Exhibitions of Mandatory Jerusalem*: A Resurgent Nahda explores the cultural and political roots of Palestine. The exhibition invites the public to discover an often little-known side of the history of the Palestinian people.
Vendredi matin, 11 h. L’atmosphère de la: Friday morning, 11 a.m. The atmosphere in McGill’s Islamic Studies Library is studious. A few students are absorbed in their reading. The wooden floor creaks softly under our feet as we enter the first space of the exhibition, accompanied by Dyala Hamzah and Nyla Matuk, founders of Maison Palestine, the organization behind the exhibition.
Nyla, écrivaine au visage fin et à la pe: Nyla, a writer with fine features and olive skin, radiates calm and gentleness. Beside her, Dyala, a historian with short white hair, is warm and has a sharp gaze. Both are of Palestinian origin. Together, they act as guides to this singular exhibition. Their eloquent vocabulary reflects their expertise and their passion for the subject.
<strong>« Une période où tout est encore: “A time when everything is still possible”
« Cette exposition redonne vie à l’histo: “This exhibition brings the history of Palestine back to life,” Dyala begins with a discreet smile. It features illustrations of Arab art and photographs from the period of colonial resistance against the British and the Zionists**, between the major Palestinian revolts of 1929 and 1936.
Elle et Nyla ont étroitement collaboré a: She and Nyla worked closely with historian and architect Nadi Abusaada, who originally conceived the exhibition at the Khalil Sakakini Cultural Centre in Ramallah, Palestine, as well as with Luzan Munayer, assistant curator. For them, bringing this project to Montréal is an act of preserving Palestinian heritage, despite the logistical challenges such an undertaking entails. “Export restrictions affecting the Palestinian territories forced Nadi to recreate the exhibition using reproductions and visual archives. So only printed materials are on display,” Dyala explains. “The original exhibition included artifacts, jewellery, paintings, printed material and many other things that we couldn’t import for this exhibition,” Nyla adds. Indeed, since October 7, 2023, Israel has imposed very strict restrictions on the movement of people and goods in the West Bank.
L’installation met de l’avant les deux g: The installation highlights the two major exhibitions of 1933 and 1934, key moments when Palestinians, then under British Mandate, showcased their culture and know-how in a surge of collective pride. “They were a kind of trade fair,” Nyla clarifies.
« Ces événements, poursuit Dyala, attira: “These events,” Dyala continues, “drew visitors from across the region. They featured industrial, artisanal and artistic products. Here, you can see all the Arab countries that took part in the exhibition,” the historian explains in front of an interactive screen.
Un panneau central rappelle que ces évén: A central panel reminds visitors that these events took place in the midst of confrontation with the Zionists and the British: despite colonial pressure, the organizers succeeded in sparking a Nahda, a true “renaissance.”
« Ces expositions ont manifesté une vigu: “These exhibitions demonstrated an economic vitality that countered attempts to hold back Palestinian development,” Dyala continues. It is an allusion to the policies put in place by the Zionist movement, particularly the Histadrut***, which in the 1920s prohibited the hiring of Palestinian labour. The goal was to consolidate a separate economy.
Du même souffle, l’historienne déclare f: In the same breath, the historian proudly declares: “And ultimately, this exhibition shows that, despite this hostile campaign against the local economy, there is an economic vitality in Palestinian society that is on display in the organization of these two fairs in 1933 and 1934.”
« C’était un moment intense de renouveau: “It was an intense moment of socio-cultural renewal,” Nyla points out. “Despite the threat of Zionist colonization, Palestinians held onto hope.”
Revenir sur une époque où tout était enc: Looking back on a time when everything was still possible seemed essential to these two women at a moment when the Palestinian territories are being constantly bombed. “There was this faith in the future, and we still believe in it today, in spite of everything and despite the current genocide,” Dyala adds.
<strong>Palace Hotel : une lutte pour l’: Palace Hotel: A Struggle for Palestinian Identity
Alors que nous nous avançons vers la sec: As we move toward the second room of the exhibition, Dyala continues: “This exhibition also explores the architectural history of Jerusalem.”
Dans une salle octogonale, entièrement e: In an octagonal room made entirely of solid wood, students linger around a central table while banners on the walls tell the story of the Palace Hotel, which hosted both the 1933 and 1934 exhibitions.
Construit en 1929 sous la direction du C: Built in 1929 under the direction of the Supreme Muslim Council and the Grand Mufti Amin al-Husseini, the Palace Hotel was designed to strengthen the Arab presence in Jerusalem. It symbolized a form of resistance, the Palestinian answer to the King David Hotel, the quintessential emblem of British and Zionist influence.
« Les deux expositions ainsi que le Pala: “The two exhibitions, as well as the Palace Hotel itself, were meant to show Arab populations around the world what they had to offer on the global market at the time,” Nyla explains. “Palestinians were then trying to build their own economy, which was suffering the effects of de-development, and continues to do so today, because of what colonialism has produced.”
Très rapidement, l’hôtel devient lui-mêm: Very quickly, the hotel itself became “a symbol of colonization par excellence,” as an exhibition panel points out. Indeed, the Supreme Muslim Council’s mismanagement of the hotel and its finances led to it being leased to the British administration. In 1936, the building was chosen to house the offices of the <l1>Peel Commission</l1>, tasked with investigating the Great Palestinian Revolt, an uprising against British policies supporting Zionist colonization. It was also at the Palace Hotel that the first lines of the 1937 plan to partition Palestine were drawn.
« L’exposition montre également comment: “The exhibition also shows how colonialism shaped the commercial and cultural environment of the time,” Nyla continues.
Aujourd’hui, l’établissement appartient: Today, the building belongs to the Waldorf Astoria chain, which has completely transformed its interior, marking a symbolic break with its past and erasing part of its history.
Avec cette exposition, Dyala et Nyla pré: With this exhibition, Dyala and Nyla offer a different perspective on Palestinian identity. They point to narratives that <l1>tend to deny the very existence of a Palestinian people</l1>, reducing them solely “to Bedouins who could just as well wander here as anywhere else,” says Dyala.
« Cette vision des choses ignore complèt: “This view completely ignores the fact that we’re talking about an urban, highly connected population that has always played a central role in the Arab world,” the historian states. For her, the exhibition is a way of restoring a more complete and more authentic image of Palestinians during a period when Arab nationalism was in full ferment. “You see an extremely tight network of Arabs, [a people] on the move across the region, whose identities are both singular and general. There is an Arab-ness, but there are also very local identities. You are Palestinian, you are Palestinian Arab, and Palestinians were convinced they were carrying this Arab renaissance at a time when it was less pronounced elsewhere,” she says.
Nyla, de son côté, voit en l’exposition: Nyla, for her part, sees the exhibition as an act of resistance against dominant media narratives. “[It] presents facts, but they are dangerous to the prevailing discourse, which has been established as a kind of smear campaign against Palestine and Palestinians.”
Dyala Hamzah et Nyla Matu, les co-fondat: Dyala Hamzah and Nyla Matuk, co-founders of Maison Palestine. Photo: Aude Simon
Selon elle, cette vision est relayée par: According to her, this view is relayed by certain Quebec academic institutions, which “prefer to secure this narrative, [even if it means] limiting access to alternative narratives.”
« On veut empêcher les gens d’être éduqu: “They want to keep people from being educated on this subject,” she says in exasperation, referring to numerous refusals to host the exhibition. “It’s fascinating... It’s fascinating and horrifying at the same time.”
De fait, organiser une telle exposition: Indeed, organizing such an exhibition was not a smooth road, the two women tell us. “It was extremely difficult to find a venue for our project. We knocked on a dozen doors, and we were told no everywhere. Finally, the Carrefour des arts et des sciences at Université de Montréal was enthusiastic about the idea,” Dyala recounts.
Toutefois, alors que le lancement était: However, while the launch was scheduled for between January and March 2024, the Faculty of Arts and Sciences cancelled the event, citing security reasons. “We were shocked to learn of this decision. For us, these security justifications are extremely flimsy,” she comments with irritation. The organizers were offered the option of postponing the exhibition to June, with no guarantee. That was an unacceptable compromise for Dyala: “In June, campuses are empty, so it would have been pointless.”
Contactée à ce sujet, l’Université de Mo: When contacted about this, Université de Montréal explained that the decision to postpone the event was made because of tensions in Montréal at the time. “Remember the fall of 2023, when demonstrations, Molotov cocktails and other hateful graffiti on the walls of Jewish schools (among others) were part of life in Montréal. At UdeM, we were not victims of these events, but the context was very volatile.”
Selon la porte-parole Geneviève O’Meara,: According to spokesperson Geneviève O’Meara, it was not possible to guarantee the security of the premises for an exhibition that was to last three months. She notes that, despite this, lectures and activities related to the tensions in the Middle East were able to take place on campus over the course of the year.
Finalement, c’est à la Bibliothèque d’ét: In the end, the exhibition found refuge at McGill University’s Islamic Studies Library. “We hadn’t planned to exhibit in a library, and obviously, the fact that it’s in the Islamic Studies Library somewhat accentuates the niche aspect of the exhibition, perhaps isolates it even more, but we are extremely happy to have had the opportunity to show it for four months,” Dyala adds with a faint smile.
« Nous avons pris des photos de tous les: “We took photos of all the available spaces to send to Nadi Abusaada,” Dyala adds. She and Nyla worked remotely with Nadi and Luzan to adapt the library’s spaces as best they could, since they weren’t designed to host this type of event. “The installation was acrobatic, even epic,” she continues, letting out a small laugh.
Pour Dyala et Nyla, exposer sur le campu: For Dyala and Nyla, exhibiting on the McGill campus carries particular significance. “It’s ironic to do it on a campus that has often exercised a certain violence toward the Palestinian solidarity movement,” says Dyala. “Security guards are everywhere, <l1>even surveilling some students</l1>,” Nyla chimes in. She points in particular to the tense atmosphere that prevailed on campus throughout 2024.
En repassant par la salle principale de: Passing back through the main room of the exhibition, I notice the guestbook lying open on a table. Visitors’ messages fill its pages, and all converge on one simple phrase: “Bravo.”
<l1>Maison Palestine</l1> est un organis: <l1>Maison Palestine</l1> is a non-profit organization (NPO) founded in January 2023 by Nyla Matuk and Dyala Hamzah, both of Palestinian origin. The NPO’s goal is to create a permanent space “dedicated to the culture, history and future of Palestine,” the two women explain. Nyla and Dyala want to organize in Montréal “more than one-off events, like festivals or occasional exhibitions, which, while valuable, lack permanence.” Their aim is to establish in the public space a “home” for Palestine that would be at once a library, a museum and an event space: a cultural centre.

* <l1>La Palestine mandataire</l1> : En: * <l1>Mandatory Palestine</l1>: In 1922, Palestine was placed under British Mandate by the League of Nations, like other former Ottoman territories. Unlike those territories, which would become independent states, Palestine was intended to host a “national home for the Jewish people,” in accordance with the 1917 Balfour Declaration. The British Mandate ended in 1948 with the creation of the State of Israel, resulting in the division of Palestine and major geopolitical upheavals in the region, notably the 1948–1949 Arab-Israeli War.
** Le sionisme est un mouvement politiqu: ** Zionism is a political movement born in the late 19th century that aimed to create a territory for the Jewish people, primarily to protect them from growing antisemitism in Europe. In 1897, at the first Zionist Congress in Basel, Switzerland, Theodor Herzl proposed in his manifesto, The Jewish State, a program for the creation of a Jewish state in Palestine, considered the “Promised Land” in Jewish tradition. This movement encouraged Jewish immigration to Palestine, leading to an increase in the Jewish population in the early 20th century, but also to mass displacements and massacres of the Arab population, already present on the territory.
*** La <l1>Histadrout</l1>, fondée en 19: *** The Histadrut, founded in 1920, is the trade union federation of Jewish workers in Palestine, then under British Mandate. It played a role in the economic and social development of the Zionist movement and in the building of the Jewish economy in Palestine, and then in Israel after 1948. The Histadrut actively promoted “Jewish labour” (Avoda Ivrit in Hebrew), a policy aimed at employing only Jewish workers in order to develop a self-sufficient economy.
